derivations.claim: Let $\widetilde\Omega=\mathbb R\times(0,h)\times\mathbb R$ and $\Lambda=\{(mL_x,0,nL_z):m,n\in\mathbb Z\}$. For $U=U_P$ in the Poiseuille case and $U=U_C$ in the Couette case, define the lifted material map for each $t$ by $\widetilde\chi^U_t(x,y,z)=(x+tU(y),y,z)$. Both profiles are smooth, so this map is $C^\infty$; its inverse is $(x-tU(y),y,z)$. It maps $\widetilde\Omega$ onto itself, fixes the $y$ coordinate, and obeys $\widetilde\chi^U_t(a+\lambda)=\widetilde\chi^U_t(a)+\lambda$ for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$. Its Jacobian matrix is $\begin{pmatrix}1&tU'(y)&0\\0&1&0\\0&0&1\end{pmatrix}$, with determinant $1>0$. Since $y$ is unchanged, $\partial_t\widetilde\chi^U_t=(U(y),0,0)=\widetilde u(t,\widetilde\chi^U_t(x,y,z))$, so each map descends to the periodic channel and has the example's velocity as its Eulerian velocity. Thus both profiles meet the material-motion hypothesis of [F1].

In the Poiseuille case, $U_P(0)=U_P(h)=0$ and $U_P''=-G/\eta$. Thus $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_x+\rho b_x=\eta U_P''+G=0$, and the other momentum components vanish, proving the steady equations and no-slip compatibility. Direct integration gives $Q_P=\int_0^hU_P(y)\,dy=Gh^3/(12\eta)$ and $\omega_{P,z}=-U_P'=-G(h-2y)/(2\eta)$.

In the Couette case, $U_C(0)=0$, $U_C(h)=V$, and $U_C''=0$, so the momentum equation holds with constant pressure and no body force; the velocity traces equal the stated wall velocities. Direct integration gives $Q_C=\int_0^hU_C(y)\,dy=Vh/2$ and $\omega_{C,z}=-U_C'=-V/h$.

By the defined squared norm $|D|^2=D:D$, for either profile $|D|^2=(U')^2/2$, hence viscous dissipation per unit streamwise/spanwise wall area is $\eta\int_0^h(U')^2\,dy$. In the Poiseuille case this is $\frac{G^2}{4\eta}\int_0^h(h-2y)^2\,dy=G^2h^3/(12\eta)$, while body-force power is $\int_0^h\rho(G/\rho)U_P\,dy=GQ_P=G^2h^3/(12\eta)$; stationary-wall power is zero. This agrees with the stationary no-slip case of [F1].

In the Couette case viscous dissipation per unit wall area is $\eta\int_0^h(V/h)^2\,dy=\eta V^2/h$. At the top wall $n=(0,1,0)$ and $\sigma n$ has tangential component $\eta(V/h)(1,0,0)$, so wall power per unit area is $g\cdot\sigma n=\eta V^2/h$; the lower wall has $g=0$. This agrees with the tangential no-slip case of [F1]. Finally, a purported periodic pressure $p_0-Gx$ changes by $-GL_x$ under $x\mapsto x+L_x$, so it is not single-valued on $\Omega$ when $G>0$; the body-force formulation in the Example avoids that incompatibility.

For either profile $u=(U(y),0,0)$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$, $\partial_tu=0$ and $(u\cdot\nabla)u=U(y)\partial_xu=0$. The only nonzero entries of $D$ are $D_{xy}=D_{yx}=U'/2$, so the only nonzero viscous shear entries are $\sigma_{xy}=\sigma_{yx}=\eta U'$, and $(\operatorname{div}\sigma)_x=-\partial_xp+\eta U''$.

Apply the material-transport identity in [F5], componentwise to $q=\rho u$, on a relatively compact neighborhood of $K$ and a time-translated interval containing $0$ at $t_0$. Because $\rho$ is constant and $\operatorname{div}u=0$, $D_t(\rho u)+(\rho u)\operatorname{div}u=\rho(\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u)$. The open-region integral compatibility in [F5] identifies the resulting compact-Jordan integrals with those over $\chi_t(V)$, so $\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho u\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(V)}\rho(\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u)\,dx$ at $t=t_0$.

By [F5], the image $\chi_t(V)$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain. The adopted Newtonian stress [F3] is $C^1$ up to its boundary by the stated field regularity, since $\overline{\chi_t(V)}$ is compactly contained in $\Omega_t$. Apply [F4] to each row of $\sigma$ to replace its traction resultant by $\int_{\chi_t(V)}\operatorname{div}\sigma\,dx$. Substitution of step 1.1 into [A1] gives $\int_{\chi_t(V)}R(t,x)\,dx=0$ for every such $V$, where $R:=\rho(\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u)-\rho b-\operatorname{div}\sigma$ is continuous. The hypotheses of [F4] hold by the stated regularity, the $C^2$ motion and [A2].

Fix $t$ and $x_0\in\Omega_t$. For all sufficiently small $r>0$, the closed ball $\overline{B_r(x_0)}$ lies in $\Omega_t$. Apply [F5]'s $C^1$-image clause to the inverse diffeomorphism $\chi_t^{-1}$ on a neighborhood of this closed ball; then $V:=\chi_t^{-1}(B_r(x_0))$ is bounded, has $C^1$ boundary, and satisfies $\overline V\Subset B$. Step 2.1 gives $\int_{B_r(x_0)}R(t,x)\,dx=0$. If any component $R_i(t,x_0)$ were positive, continuity would make it positive on some sufficiently small ball and force its integral to be positive; if negative, the integral would be negative. Both contradict the zero integral, so $R_i(t,x_0)=0$ for each component. Thus $R=0$ throughout $\Omega_t$, which is the claimed local momentum equation.
